name: Morning Blue
lede: Morning Blue is a pale, blue-grey green, recorded in Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary as first used in 1916, one of more than two dozen dictionary names the ISCC-NBS system later filed together in a single block.

sections.title: One name among two dozen in a block
sections.body:
Our library credits the earliest record to Maerz and Paul's 1930 color dictionary, which dates the name itself to 1916 [1]. The ISCC-NBS system filed it in 1955 as part of block 149, "pale green," alongside more than two dozen other dictionary names including Abyss, Aqua Grey, Pacific and Rabbit, all judged close enough in hue, lightness and chroma to share one block [1]. Morning Blue itself measures 1.2 units from that block's centre [1].

Its nearest named neighbor is [[light-celandine-green|Light Celandine Green]], only 3.0 units away and read as almost the same color [2]. [[dark-bluish-glaucous|Dark Bluish Glaucous]], [[grey-celadon|Greenish Sage]] and [[grey-celadon|Grey Celadon]] each sit 4.3 units out, greener [2]. In print, the phrase "morning blue" rose fastest in the 1890s and peaked in the 2010s, by Google Books count across all senses of the words [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Our archive finds this color in 389 of 23,781 paintings, about 1.6 percent, as photographed; the within-painting lens finds it in 229 [3]. It is more common than 71 percent of the named colors [3]. It peaks in the 1900s, at 1.6 percent of the 1,674 paintings from that century (26 paintings), 1.8 times the expected rate [3]. Inside a painting it most often plays a light, 38 percent of its 229 occurrences [3]. Gustav Klimt is its most devoted painter, using it in 4 of his 50 works here, 4.6 times the baseline rate (3.6 times as photographed) [3]. It shares canvases with Pale Olive Grey and Sand more than chance, at 5.0 and 2.2 times the expected rate [3]. These are photographs of varnished paintings; a color match is not a pigment identification [3].
